newsitem.title: USA: Russian Eurobond sells on novelty, diversification.
newsitem.headline: Russian Eurobond sells on novelty, diversification.

text.p: Eager global investors are expected to lap up the first Russian Eurobond with gusto worthy of hungry capitalists sneered at by former communists.

U.S. analysts say the surprising level of interest in Russia's first international debt issue in 80 years appeals to the appetite of portfolio managers, who, until now bound by covenants, could not own when-issued Vnesh loans or Minfin bonds.

"For some fund managers, this is the first opportunity for them to own any Russian papers," said Frank Fernandez, portfolio manager of Global Emerging Markets Advisors. "The novelty value alone will drive the prices up."

He said one factor making the Russian Eurobond a "must have" for some investors is the stellar performance of outstanding Russian debt denominated in foreign currencies which, according to J.P. Morgan Emerging Markets Composite Index, have risen 120 percent this year.

Since the roadshow began two weeks ago, all of the $300 million to $500 million bond had been placed, and demand -- expected to be up to five times oversubscribed -- was driving yields towards 300 basis points over U.S. Treasuries from 365 basis points earlier.
"We think it will be a blowout," said Peter Wilby, senior portfolio manager of Salomon Bothers Asset Management.
Russia received a credit-rating of BB-minus from Standard and Poor's and Ba2 from Moody's Investors Service Inc.
Ironically, problems with the Minfin bonds, some of which have been frozen pending investigation of theft, made Russian Eurobonds more attractive.
"There is a space on the yield curve (for the two-to-five-year Eurobond), comparable to tranche 3 of the Minfin bond," said a portfolio manager. "But you don't have to fiddle with the custody issue."
Positive momentum should power the Eurobond higher on the secondary market at least through the end of the year, he said.
But for many investors who have been veterans in the Russian debt market, the Eurobond does not top their list.
"We are not planning to buy the bond," said a money manager. "The BB-minus credit rating puts Russia at the top end of the expected credit range, which will give it little room for upgrade soon."
Fernandez prefers to stick to the Russian domestic GKO market for its high yield, given the Eurobond will likely be too pricey when it finally comes to market.

Thanks to the segmentation of investors, the fragile condition of the Russian budget and its financing is barely audible in the soaring chorus of paen to Russia's bright economic future, said Vladimir Kvint, head of Russian investments at Arthur Anderson.
"The Eurobond issue should help determine the price of borrowing," he said. "The paper is more a promotional confidence-building excercise than a means of raising signficant funds for the budget."
It remains to be seen if the hearty reception of the Eurobond will open the spigot of direct foreign investment into Russia, he noted.
